paras: The threatened lynching of Miles Mayo took place at Roslyn, Washington, in early August 1890, when talk of lynching followed Mayo's arrest for stabbing a white liveryman in a quarrel over a horse. Town officials took Mayo, a Black man, out of the Roslyn jail to Ellensburg for safe keeping, and he was not harmed. Papers on the Pacific coast treated the case as a near "race war" because Black residents declared they would avenge Mayo if he were lynched.

Some versions of the wire story set the quarrel among Roslyn's miners, adding that "a bitter hatred exists between white and black miners." The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's headline called Mayo a "Black Minor" [miner].

According to a dispatch from Ellensburg dated August 5, the trouble began "Yesterday shortly after noon," when Pat Harvy, a white livery keeper, and Mayo, "a colored man," quarreled about a horse. In that account Harvy struck Mayo first, and Mayo drew a pocket knife and stabbed him in the lung, a wound the dispatch called "probably fatal." A shorter wire report named the liveryman "Polheny" and said only that Mayo stabbed and "dangerously wounded" him in a quarrel over a horse.

Deputy Sheriff Mat Miller arrested Mayo at once and put him in the city jail. When "talk of lynching" was heard, Mayor Miller, the deputy sheriff and City Marshal Beal took him out of the jail and brought him to Ellensburg, where he was jailed. The reports do not describe a crowd at the jail or any attempt to seize him, and a Salem paper added that "all is quiet now."

Black residents of Roslyn, the wire said, declared that if Mayo were lynched they would avenge his death. The longer dispatch went further, saying they were determined he should not be lynched and "threatened to clean out the town," so that an attempt would have brought "a terrible row."

The next night another row broke out at Roslyn, in which George Oglesby shot Marshal Brown, both described as colored; an Ellensburg dispatch said the cause was believed to be "the stabbing affray of Monday." The same dispatch reported that the stabbed liveryman was "doing well, and will probably recover." No report of a charge, hearing or trial of Mayo was found in the coverage.

The story reached the press through two Ellensburg dispatches and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, and all of the coverage found is from white papers in the Pacific states. The short wire ran on August 6 in the Los Angeles Herald as "A Lynching Averted" and in the San Francisco Morning Call and the Sacramento Record-Union as "Stabbing Affray." A rewrite naming the conflict as one between "white and black miners" circulated in coast-news columns from Carson City on August 8 to Lebanon, Oregon, and Shelton, Washington, as late as August 22.

The longer dispatch, carried by the Albany State Rights Democrat as "A Tragedy at Ellensburg" and by The Dalles Times-Mountaineer as "RACE WAR AT ROSLYN," gave the fuller story; The Dalles text closed that "a terrible tragedy was undoubtedly avoided." The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's front page put the case under the deck "Whites and Negroes at Roslyn on the Verge of Bloody War," saying the "Black Minor" [miner] had stabbed a white man fatally and "Narrowly Escapes Lynching." Most papers called Mayo "a negro" and framed the danger as much in the Black residents' threat of reprisal as in the lynching talk itself. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The longer dispatch and the Seattle follow-up place the stabbing on Monday, August 4, while the short wire said "this afternoon" in an August 5 dispatch and a Carson City rewrite said "Tuesday." The two dispatches also named the liveryman differently, as Pat Harvy and as "Polheny," with further spellings in reprints. Early reports called the wound probably fatal, but the later Seattle report said the man would probably recover.

bases: After Mayo, a colored man, stabbed a white liveryman, 'talk of lynching' led officers to move him from the Roslyn jail to Ellensburg; no attempt on him is reported (A12, A10, A4, A1).

accounts.label: Short Ellensburg wire
accounts.gist: Mayo stabbed and dangerously wounded a liveryman in a quarrel over a horse 'this afternoon'; he was jailed at Ellensburg through fear of lynching, and negroes vowed to avenge him if lynched.

accounts.label: Longer Ellensburg dispatch
accounts.gist: Harvy struck Mayo first and Mayo stabbed him in the lung; the mayor, deputy sheriff and marshal took Mayo to Ellensburg when lynching talk was heard, and armed conflict was averted because Black residents were determined he should not be lynched.

accounts.label: Seattle Post-Intelligencer
accounts.gist: Called Roslyn 'on the Verge of Bloody War'; a day later reported a second shooting tied to the stabbing and that the stabbed man would probably recover.

framing.detail: California papers ran the short wire as 'A Lynching Averted' or 'Stabbing Affray', calling Mayo 'a negro' and noting 'Bitter hatred exists between whites and blacks'.

The Dalles Times-Mountaineer headed the longer dispatch 'RACE WAR AT ROSLYN' and wrote that an attempted lynching would have meant 'a terrible row' because the negroes 'threatened to clean out the town'.
The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's front-page deck described whites and negroes 'on the Verge of Bloody War' and a 'Black Minor' [miner] who 'Narrowly Escapes Lynching'.
